# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–17 (Complete – Updated 131)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Spring of fifth year** (Chapter 17 opening). Winter 1815-16 passed. Waterloo campaign: 16 June 1815 morning—regiment receives marching orders; afternoon/evening—cannonading; by 10 PM—Belgian hussar Regulus arrives with disaster tales; by dawn 17 June—wounded return; afternoon 17 June—victory news spreads; 18 June (Sunday)—religious services. **Critical event (26 March 1816)**: Rebecca delivers son and heir to Rawdon. **Spring 1816**: Pitt marries Lady Jane at Brighton (hastily arranged by Miss Crawley); they move into Miss Crawley's house. Lady Southdown assumes control. Miss Crawley dies (spring/early summer 1816). George Osborne's letter (written 16 June before dawn) delivered approximately three weeks after 18 June—early July 1815. **Late autumn 1815**: Mr. Osborne announces trip to Belgium; church incident with George's monument; confrontation with Colonel Dobbin in Brussels. **Chapter 17 timeline**: Approximately 3-4 years after Paris establishment; Rawdon and Rebecca now in Curzon Street, May Fair, London.
- **Locations**: London (Russell Square, Thames Street, Slaughters' hotel, Gray's Inn Square, Hulker and Bullock bankers, Curzon Street May Fair, Fulham), Brussels, Belgium, Waterloo battlefield, Brighton, Southampton, Paris, Faubourg St. Germain, Coldcombe hill farms, Dunholt, Calais, Dunkirk, various other towns.

## Main Characters

**Captain William Dobbin (now Colonel)**
- **Promoted to Major, then Colonel** after second Major's death at Waterloo. Greatly respected as best officer and cleverest man. Secret, unrequited adoration of Amelia. Before campaign: instructed Jos to watch over Amelia. **Late autumn 1815**: In Brussels with recovering regiment. **Confrontation with Mr. Osborne**: Encountered Osborne in Brussels street; followed to Hotel du Parc; pleaded for forgiveness of Amelia and unborn child. **Osborne's refusal**: Complete rejection of reconciliation. **Dobbin's role**: Brought Amelia back to England to her mother's house in Fulham when Mrs. O'Dowd received summons. **Godfather to Georgy**: Became godfather of infant; purchases gifts constantly (cups, spoons, toys). **Chapter 17 status**: Visits Amelia's house daily for hours; visits Mr. Clapp's family regularly. Brings presents almost daily—recently wooden horse, drum, trumpet. Upon intimate moment with Amelia and child, experienced crushing realization of hopeless love. Knows there is no place for him in her heart despite her maternal affection. Gently bears his fate with fatal perspicuity; content to remain. Amelia laughs when he arrives, holds out hand, kisses him with "hopeless kindness." Her parents appear to encourage him without effect.

**George Osborne**
- **DEAD at Waterloo (16 June 1815, though monument inscription states 18 June)** — discrepancy noted. Married Amelia late April without father's consent; disinherited. Received £2,000 in 4 percent annuities and £100/year widow's allowance for Amelia. At Brussels: carried on desperate flirtation with Rebecca; sent letter and bouquet after campaign began. Departed 16 June with regiment. **Written final letter before daybreak 16 June** to father (delivered July via Dobbin's officer): farewell before great battle; imploration to provide for Amelia and possible child; contrition for irregularities; thanks; promise to act worthily. Letter sealed with sham coat of arms and "Pax in bello" motto. **The seal itself was robbed from George's dead body on battlefield**. **Monument erected** in church with Osborne arms, inscription stating death 18 June, aged 28, "while fighting for his king and country in the glorious victory of Waterloo. Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori." Depicts Britannia weeping over urn, broken sword, couchant lion.

**Amelia Osborne**
- **Widow and Mother**—George killed at Waterloo. Delivered infant Georgy (godchild to Colonel Dobbin), scarcely six months old. Status: receives £100/year widow's allowance; holds £2,000 in 4 percent annuities. **Health**: "Very bad" condition after Waterloo; "out of her mind like for six weeks or more"; life and reason "shaken by the blow." However, recovery underway by time Dobbin brought her to England. **Chapter 17 status**: Living with parents in Fulham; fully recovered and devoted entirely to mothering Georgy. Her existence is maternal caress; she envelops child with love and worship. Nurses, dresses, lives upon him; drove away all nurses; allows only her own hand to touch him. Considers allowing Dobbin occasionally to dandle him greatest favour. Shows bright maternal pleasure when infant's hands close round Dobbin's finger. Laughs when Major arrives; kisses him with hopeless kindness. Recovery complete.

**Captain Rawdon Crawley (now Lieutenant-Colonel, then Colonel)**
- **Married to Rebecca**. Made last dispositions for Rebecca before campaign. Rode by General's side; gallantry mentioned in Gazette; promoted to Lieutenant-Colonel; awarded C.B. **Paris period (3-4 years post-Waterloo)**: Quitted Guards and sold out of army. Mustachios and title of Colonel only relics of military profession. Lived comfortably at Paris with Rebecca on "nothing per annum" for 2-3 years through undisclosed financial ingenuity. Owned skills in gambling and card games. **Gambling activities**: Regularly hosted card-tables at private evening reunions in Paris house. Played successfully with young officers (Green of Rifles, Blackstone of Hussars, Count Punter of Hanoverian Cavalry). **Incident with Colonel O'Dowd**: Loud violent fracas at Cafe de Paris; ladies engaged on both sides; Mrs. O'Dowd snapped fingers in Rebecca's face, called Rawdon "no betther than a black-leg"; Colonel Crawley challenged Colonel O'Dowd, C.B. Commander-in-Chief intervened (pistols "which he shot Captain Marker" were ready); no duel occurred. **Rebecca's intervention**: Went on knees to General Tufto; Crawley narrowly escaped being sent back to England; did not play except with civilians for some weeks after. **Recent assessment**: Rebecca convinced Rawdon that gambling as income was precarious; after few nights of suppers, gentlemen grew tired of play with him. **News of Miss Crawley's death**: Upon news aunt was dying, Colonel hastily departed Paris for Calais, then diverted to Dunkirk and Brussels (preferred Belgian city to noisy capitals; actually owed more money at London than Paris). **Current status (Chapter 17)**: Busy arranging affairs of inheritance in London; wife and child to follow; planning to take better lodgings.

**Rebecca Sharp (Mrs. Rebecca Rawdon Crawley)**
- **Brussels post-departure**: Secured financial independence through horse sales to Jos, Rawdon's effects sales, stitched-away trinkets, bills, bank-notes. **Paris period (3-4 years post-Waterloo)**: Flourished in polite life; accommodates herself to fashionable life as if ancestors were people of fashion for centuries; merits place of honour in Vanity Fair through wit, talent, energy. **By 26 March 1816**: Delivered son and heir. Wrote all letters to Miss Crawley (attributed to Rawdon), sent war relics. **Miss Crawley's fury**: Made use of Miss Crawley's name to gain Parisian society entree. When discovered, Miss Crawley's fury "beyond bounds"; dictated furious answer to Briggs in English, repudiating Rebecca entirely as "most artful and dangerous person." Duchess of X (Parisian correspondent) did not understand English and reported to Rebecca that Miss Crawley sent "charming letter" with "benevolent things." **Parisian society success**: Achieved very smart and leading position; welcomed at distinguished houses of restored French nobility; English men of fashion courted her to disgust of their wives, who could not bear parvenue. For some months, salons of Faubourg St. Germain and Court delighted and perhaps intoxicated her; may have slighted honest young military men during period of elation. **Gambling house reputation**: Much to her annoyance, Rawdon's passion for dice flourished at her reunions. She spoke of his passion with deepest grief, besought young fellows never to touch box, wept whole nights when young Green lost considerable sum, went on knees to Rawdon to remit debts and burn acknowledgements. Rawdon refused—he owed as much to Blackstone and Count Punter; Green must pay; burning IOUs was child's play. Her house began to have unfortunate reputation among officers. **Son and heir**: After amiable fashion of French mothers, placed him out at nurse in village near Paris with numerous foster-brothers in wooden shoes. Father (Rawdon) would ride over to see him; paternal heart glowed seeing him rosy, dirty, shouting lustily, making mud-pies. Rebecca did not care much to visit; once infant spoiled dove-coloured pelisse of hers; preferred nurse's caresses to mamma's; when finally quitted nurse, cried loudly for hours, consoled only by promise of returning next day; nurse awaited child's return quite anxiously. **Chapter 17 journey to London**: Upon news of Miss Crawley's death, ordered intense mourning for herself and little Rawdon. Departed Paris in landlord's carriage with French bonne and child. **Negotiation with creditors**: Object was to effect compromise with Rawdon's numerous creditors by offering ninepence or shilling per pound dividend, securing his return to own country. Showed creditors that offered sum was all husband's available capital; convinced them Rawdon preferred perpetual Continental retirement to English residence with unsettled debts; proved no other money sources and no larger dividend possible. Brought creditors unanimously to accept proposals; purchased with fifteen hundred pounds ready money more than ten times that amount of debts. General Tufto furious when she departed; Mrs. Brent furious with him; Lieutenant Spooney cut to heart; landlord got ready best apartments for her return. Trunks she left in landlord's charge (especially recommended by her) not found particularly valuable when opened later.

**Jos Sedley**
- **Fled Brussels** 16 June toward Ghent road on horseback with Isidor, abandoning Amelia and company. Mrs. O'Dowd made scornful remarks. **Current status (late autumn 1815)**: Widow Amelia's available source of financial aid, though willingness uncertain.

**Miss Crawley (at Brighton, then with Pitt)**
- Worth approximately **seventy thousand pounds**. **Forced marriage of Pitt and Lady Jane**: Upon learning of Rebecca's pregnancy and Rawdon's son (26 March 1816), rage reached height. Summoned Pitt and Lady Southdown, requested immediate marriage celebration. Announced intention to allow couple £1,000/year during lifetime; bulk of property to settle upon Pitt and Lady Jane upon death. Mr. Waxy (solicitor) ratified deeds; marriage celebrated with Bishop. **After marriage**: Pitt and Lady Jane moved into her house. Affection for Lady Jane grew so strong she could not part with her favourite. **Dominated by Lady Southdown**: Reigned over entire family—Pitt, Lady Jane, Miss Crawley, Briggs, Bowls, Firkin. Pitilessly dosed them with tracts and medicine; dismissed Creamer; installed Rodgers; stripped Miss Crawley of authority. **Death**: Died spring/early summer 1816 during Lady Southdown's domination. Lady Jane supported her kindly in final days.

**Mr. Pitt Crawley (Bar of England)**
- **Married Lady Jane** (spring 1816, hastily arranged). **Now living in Miss Crawley's house** with wife. Receives £1,000/year during her lifetime with wife; bulk settles upon them upon her death. Greatly annoyed by humours of aunt and mother-in-law Lady Southdown. Lady Southdown reigns over household; Pitt conceived himself "most injured character." Diplomatic strategy fully succeeded—he is Miss Crawley's favoured nephew.

**Lady Jane Sheepshanks/Crawley**
- **Married Pitt Crawley** (spring 1816). **Living in Miss Crawley's house**. Receives £1,000/year during Miss Crawley's lifetime (shared with Pitt); bulk settles upon her upon Miss Crawley's death. Remains kind and artless; Miss Crawley clung to her as favourite; supported her kindly in final days.

**Mr. Osborne (Elder)**
- George's father in Russell Square. Placed household in mourning upon learning George died; cancelled parties; closed house front. Made no communication to Mr. Bullock (future son-in-law). **Late autumn 1815**: Announced trip to Belgium. **In Brussels**: Visited hotel garden; sought soldiers from --th regiment; paid guinea to wounded convalescent to bring Sergeant to Hotel du Parc. **Confrontation with Dobbin**: Dobbin pleaded for forgiveness of Amelia and child. **Osborne's response**: Broke into rhapsody of self-praise and imprecations, swore never to recognize Amelia as George's wife or speak to her, stated he was "a man of his word" and would "stick to to the last day of my life." Complete refusal of reconciliation. Soldiers feasted on generosity from his "proud purse of mourning."

**Other Characters**
- **Mrs. O'Dowd**: Spent five hours by Amelia's side during cannonading; distinguished herself at Waterloo; Major became Colonel and C.B.; received peremptory summons forcing her to quit Amelia; confronted Rebecca at Cafe de Paris.
- **Sir William Dobbin (Alderman)**: Called upon Mr. Osborne senior approximately three weeks after 18 June with pale, agitated face; delivered George's sealed letter.
- **Osborne's Sisters**: At church when monument agitated their nerves; clothed in deep black; wondered whether father would forgive Mrs. George; anxious regarding recognition as family daughter.
- **Mr. Clapp (honest landlord)**: Fulham resident; Dobbin visits his family regularly.
- **Little Mary (Clapp's daughter)**: Young girl favourite with Amelia; acts as "Major Sugarplums."
- **Tom Stubble, Pauline, Isidor, Towzer, Sergeant, James Crawley (Jim), General Tufto, Mrs. Brent, Lieutenant Spooney, Blackstone, Count Punter, Green (Rifles), Colonel O'Dowd**: Status continued from previous summary.

## Critical Facts and Status
- **George's Monument Discrepancy**: Inscription states 18 June 1815; actual death 16 June 1815.
- **Amelia's Complete Recovery**: Fully recovered, devoted entirely to mothering Georgy in Fulham with parents.
- **Dobbin's Hopeless Love**: Recognizes fatal perspicuity that no place for him in Amelia's heart, entirely absorbed in motherhood. Gently bears fate, visiting daily, bringing gifts.
- **Rawdon and Rebecca's Financial Success**: Lived comfortably on "nothing per annum" in Paris 2-3 years through undisclosed arrangements. Gambling and creditor negotiations funded London activities. Rebecca negotiated creditors down through fifteen hundred pounds to cover debts exceeding fifteen thousand pounds.
- **Miss Crawley's Property Secured**: Successfully settled approximately seventy thousand pounds to Pitt and Lady Jane through forced marriage arrangement; property protected from Rawdon and Rebecca.
